title: Why Lightning Arrives Before Thunder
hook: The sky flashes, then a beat of silence, then the boom. That gap is a race you can actually measure.
description: A short why-it-happens explainer of the delay between lightning and thunder, from the speed of light versus sound to counting seconds for distance.

scenes.vo: A storm flashes across the sky, and the boom shows up a beat later, like the sound got left behind.
scenes.caption: The flash comes first. The boom arrives a beat late.
scenes.whyArt: wide establishing shot of a lightning strike over a dark horizon

scenes.vo: It feels like thunder is just slow to start, as if the sky takes its own sweet time to rumble.
scenes.caption: It feels like thunder just takes its time to start.
scenes.whyArt: simple two-object sketch: a quick flash and a lagging sound wave

scenes.vo: Light and sound both leave that strike together. Light nearly instant. Sound crawls through the air.
scenes.caption: Light and sound leave together. Sound crawls, light races.
scenes.whyArt: close-in diagram of one strike emitting fast light and slow pressure waves

scenes.vo: Count the seconds between flash and bang. Every five of them is about a mile of air the sound crossed.
scenes.caption: Count the seconds. Every five is roughly a mile away.
scenes.whyArt: worked-example panel: a stopwatch counting to a distant thunderclap

scenes.vo: So you see lightning first because light outruns sound, not because the thunder started late.
scenes.caption: You see it first because light outruns sound.
scenes.whyArt: comparison: the instant light beam versus the slow rolling sound wave
